cases.abstract: Small demonstration sets leave visual imitation policies without corrective supervision when execution errors carry them away from expert trajectories. DMD supplies that supervision by pairing synthesized wrist-camera views with actions directed toward a later expert pose. A pretrained conditional diffusion model is adapted using task demonstrations, exploratory play, or both; camera poses reconstructed from image sequences condition the new views and determine their action labels. Targeting a later frame reduces backward-pointing labels when a generated pose has already passed the next demonstrated pose. Evaluations cover pushing, stacking, pouring, shirt hanging, and cup arrangement with unseen objects in a new environment. With 24 task demonstrations, DMD succeeds in all ten apple-pushing trials, compared with three for behavior cloning. With eight task demonstrations and a generator adapted only on play data, success is 80% versus 20%. Augmenting Diffusion Policy raises cup-arrangement success from 4/25 to 16/25 on five unseen cups in a new laboratory, with both policies receiving rectified, center-cropped images. The results support using generated recovery supervision to improve execution and transfer within the tested settings, provided deviations remain recoverable; irreversible spills cannot be corrected by returning to an expert pose.
cases.methods: DMD's central operation is to turn an unrecorded camera viewpoint into a labeled correction, rather than add an image whose action is unknown. Camera poses reconstructed from demonstration sequences provide image pairs and their relative transforms for adapting a pretrained view-synthesis diffusion model; the latent-image codebook remains fixed. A small random displacement then specifies a virtual camera pose, from which the model synthesizes an observation. The action label is computed from that virtual pose to a later pose on the original expert trajectory, not merely back to the source image. If the virtual camera has passed the next demonstrated pose, targeting that pose would direct the robot backward. Using the third future frame reduces this overshooting risk. Training on these generated pairs alongside the demonstrations adds supervision for returning toward task progress without requiring an expert to act at each sampled deviation.
cases.results: Pouring tests whether supervision around perturbed views improves robot execution, rather than only prediction on recorded trajectories. With 49 task demonstrations and 16 play trajectories used to adapt the generator, DMD achieves 80% task success, versus 0% for behavior cloning in the same randomized pairwise test. The baseline often rotates the source cup without bringing it closer to the receiving cup, so positional drift grows during pouring. DMD's higher success is consistent with better correction of that drift. In a separate randomized comparison, adapting the generator only on task demonstrations yields 70% success for DMD versus 30% for behavior cloning. This second contrast supports an augmentation benefit without play data. It does not isolate the value of play: the two tests have different baseline rates and may differ in lighting or other conditions, making the 80% versus 70% comparison insufficient for that attribution. The recovery assumption also matters here, since returning to an expert pose cannot retrieve beans already spilled.
cases.notes: Abstract comparisons: Table IIa and IV-A4 establish ten-trial pushing results; eight demonstrations train the policy, while play data adapt the pretrained generator. Table V and IV-E compare five unseen cups in a new lab using a retrained rectified-image baseline. Methods III-C links virtual-camera geometry to future-pose supervision, without guaranteeing physical recovery. Results IV-C/Table IV support both pairwise pouring improvements, not an isolated play-data effect; baseline rates differ across tests. Keep the recoverability condition in prose because spilled beans invalidate a geometric return as task recovery.

cases.abstract: Fine bimanual manipulation requires demonstrations with precise control and policies that avoid accumulating errors over high-frequency trajectories. ALOHA provides an open-source teleoperation platform within a $20,000 budget, using joint-space mapping between leader and follower arms, customized parallel-jaw grippers, and four cameras. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) learns future sequences of joint-position targets rather than isolated commands, shortening the effective decision horizon. Querying the policy every timestep and combining overlapping predictions for that same timestep incorporates fresh visual observations without abrupt switches between chunks; conditional variational training models variation in human demonstrations. Evaluation covers two simulated and six hardware tasks, with 50 demonstrations per hardware task except 100 for Thread Velcro. In 25-trial hardware evaluations, ACT's reported final-stage success rates are 88% for opening a sliding ziploc bag and 96% for battery insertion, versus zero for four baselines at those stages. A six-participant study finds faster teleoperation at 50Hz than at 5Hz. Yet Thread Velcro reaches only 20% final-stage success, and initial candy-unwrapping trials produce no complete successes in ten attempts. Together, the platform and policy enable several evaluated fine-manipulation behaviors while leaving perception and force-capacity limitations.
cases.methods: ACT predicts chunks of absolute joint targets from four camera images and follower joint positions, reducing the effective horizon of high-frequency demonstrations. Labels use leader commands rather than follower motion: the difference between the command and the tracked position determines applied force through the motor controllers. During training, a conditional variational encoder maps a demonstrated chunk and proprioception to a latent style variable. The transformer policy reconstructs the chunk while regularization encourages a Gaussian prior, allowing human variation to be represented during learning. At deployment, the encoder is discarded and the latent variable is set to zero. Crucially, chunk prediction does not require withholding observations until execution ends: the policy is queried every timestep, and exponential weights combine overlapping predictions for that execution time. Averaging predictions for one time index retains observation updates without blending neighboring actions that may require different targets.
cases.results: ACT's ablations show that sequence prediction and modeling human variability address different parts of the learning problem. With temporal ensembling disabled, average success across two simulated tasks with scripted and human demonstrations rises from 1% for one-step chunks to 44% for 100-step chunks. Longer chunks slightly lower success, consistent with a tradeoff between shortening the horizon and retaining reactive control. Chunking also improves BC-ConvMLP and VINN, so its benefit is not confined to ACT's transformer architecture. In a separate ablation averaged over the two simulated tasks, removing conditional variational training reduces success on human data from 35.3% to 2%, but scarcely changes performance on scripted data. That contrast supports the objective's role in handling demonstration variability. Temporal ensembling has a smaller and less consistent effect: with each setting separately tuned, it adds 3.3 percentage points for ACT and four for BC-ConvMLP, but reduces VINN's performance. These comparisons favor modeling coherent action sequences, but do not support applying prediction averaging indiscriminately.
cases.notes: Abstract III/Table II: retain ALOHA's hardware contribution and label ACT's outcomes as final-stage rates. Slide Ziploc's pinch rate exceeds its grasp rate; query whether stage counts are independent before claiming joint trajectory completion. Results VI-A/B: chunking, variational training, and ensembling comparisons have different aggregation scopes; ensembling settings are separately tuned. Main hardware comparisons use one seed and 25 rollouts, simulation three seeds with 50 evaluations each; do not assign those counts to ablations. VI-C/E's 5Hz condition sends interpolated targets at 50Hz. Appendix F's initial candy result is 0/10; the later protocol opens 3/5 candies with ten trials per candy. Reconstruction-loss reporting remains inconsistent between implementation and pseudocode.
